q: The size of an adult human heart is roughly that of a:
o: Clenched fist of the same person
x: The adult heart is about the size of the person's own closed fist. A walnut or bean is far too small, and a football far too large.

q: The average mass of a healthy adult human heart is about:
x: An adult heart weighs roughly 250 to 350 g, so about 300 g. 30 g is far too light, and 1.5 kg is closer to the mass of the liver.

q: The narrow space between the two layers of the pericardium is filled with:
x: The pericardial cavity between the two pericardial layers contains a thin film of pericardial fluid, which lets the heart move with little friction. It contains no air or blood.

q: The chambers of the human heart that receive blood returning in the veins are the:
x: The two atria are the receiving chambers: veins empty into them. The ventricles are the pumping chambers that send blood into the arteries.

q: The superior vena cava brings deoxygenated blood to the heart from the:
x: The superior vena cava drains the upper part of the body: head, neck and arms. Blood from the lower body comes through the inferior vena cava, and from the lungs through the pulmonary veins.

q: The inferior vena cava returns blood to the right atrium from the:
o: Lower parts of the body, such as the abdomen and legs
x: The inferior vena cava collects blood from the parts of the body below the heart. The head and arms drain into the superior vena cava.

q: Just after it leaves the heart, the pulmonary trunk divides into the:
x: The pulmonary trunk splits into a right and a left pulmonary artery, one to each lung. Pulmonary veins bring blood back, and coronary arteries branch from the aorta.

q: Backflow of blood from the aorta into the left ventricle is prevented by the:
x: The aortic semilunar valve lies at the base of the aorta. The bicuspid valve guards the left atrium–ventricle opening, and the pulmonary semilunar valve guards the pulmonary trunk.

q: Each semilunar valve of the human heart is made of:
o: Two flaps held by chordae tendineae
Four flaps held by papillary muscles
x: Semilunar valves have three pocket-shaped (half-moon) cusps and no chordae tendineae. Flaps tied by chordae tendineae belong to the atrioventricular valves.

q: In a healthy adult heart, which two chambers contain oxygenated blood?
x: Oxygenated blood from the lungs enters the left atrium and passes to the left ventricle. The whole right side carries deoxygenated blood from the body.

q: The pointed lower tip of the heart, formed mainly by the left ventricle, is called the:
x: The cone-shaped heart has a broad base above, where the great vessels attach, and a pointed apex below, formed by the left ventricle.

q: Cardiac muscle cells of the heart wall are joined end to end by:
o: Tendons, which attach them to the ribs
Chordae tendineae, which hold them in place
Intercalated discs, which let impulses pass quickly from cell to cell
x: Intercalated discs join neighbouring cardiac muscle cells and let the impulse spread rapidly, so the muscle contracts as one unit. Chordae tendineae belong to the valves.

q: Which description fits the muscle of the heart wall?
x: Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle, but its fibres branch and it is involuntary. Unstriated spindle-shaped cells describe smooth muscle.

q: A blood clot blocks a branch of a coronary artery. The direct result is that:
o: Blood can no longer enter the right atrium
Part of the heart muscle is starved of oxygen and may die
x: Coronary arteries supply the myocardium itself. A blockage cuts off oxygen to the muscle it supplies, which can die (a heart attack). The chambers, valves and lungs are not directly blocked.

q: How many valves guard the openings of the chambers of the human heart?
o: Two: one on each side of the heart
Four: two atrioventricular and two semilunar
Six: one for each great vessel
x: There are four heart valves: tricuspid and bicuspid (atrioventricular), and the aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves.

q: The pulmonary circulation begins in one chamber of the heart and ends in another. These chambers are the:
x: Blood leaves the right ventricle in the pulmonary trunk, passes through the lungs and returns in the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. The systemic circulation runs from left ventricle to right atrium.

q: Which blood vessel is NOT directly connected to the heart?
x: The hepatic portal vein runs from the gut to the liver and never reaches the heart. The aorta, pulmonary trunk and superior vena cava all open into heart chambers.

q: The tricuspid and bicuspid valves are together called the:
x: Both valves lie between an atrium and a ventricle, so they are the atrioventricular (AV) valves. Semilunar valves guard the aorta and pulmonary trunk.

q: The space in the thorax between the two lungs, in which the heart lies, is called the:
x: The heart sits in the mediastinum, the central region of the thorax between the lungs. The pleural cavities surround the lungs, and the peritoneal cavity is in the abdomen.

q: If the pulmonary semilunar valve does not close properly, blood will leak back:
o: From the pulmonary trunk into the right ventricle when the ventricles relax
From the right ventricle into the right atrium when the ventricles contract
From the aorta into the left ventricle when the ventricles relax
From the left atrium into the pulmonary veins when the atria contract
x: The pulmonary semilunar valve lies between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk and should close when the ventricles relax. A leaky valve lets blood flow back into the right ventricle at that time.

q: Which pairing of a heart chamber with a vessel connected to it is correct?
x: The right ventricle pumps into the pulmonary trunk. The aorta leaves the left ventricle, the pulmonary veins enter the left atrium, and the venae cavae enter the right atrium.

q: Which is the correct order of the layers of the heart wall, from outside to inside?
x: The thin epicardium covers the outside, the thick muscular myocardium is in the middle, and the endocardium lines the chambers.

q: Compared with the three-chambered heart of a frog, the four-chambered human heart:
o: Has only one atrium receiving all the blood
Pumps blood through the body in a single circuit
Keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood completely separate
Has no valves between atria and ventricles
x: A complete septum and two ventricles keep oxygenated and deoxygenated blood fully apart in humans. A frog's single ventricle allows some mixing.

q: When the muscle of the ventricles relaxes and the ventricles refill with blood, they are said to be in:
x: Relaxation of a heart chamber is diastole, and contraction is systole. The chambers fill with blood during diastole.

q: Out of each 0.8-second heartbeat, the contraction of the atria takes about:
x: Of the 0.8 second cycle, atrial systole takes about 0.1 second, ventricular systole about 0.3 second and complete diastole about 0.4 second.

q: If someone's pulse is 60 per minute, how long does each heartbeat take?
x: One cycle lasts 60 seconds ÷ 60 beats = 1.0 second. The figure 0.8 second applies to a rate of 75 beats per minute.

q: To pump 6 litres each minute at 80 beats, how much blood must one ventricle eject with every beat?
x: Stroke volume = cardiac output ÷ heart rate = 6000 mL ÷ 80 = 75 mL per beat.

q: Stroke volume is the:
o: Volume of blood pumped by both ventricles in one minute
Number of heartbeats in one minute
Volume of blood left in a ventricle after it contracts
Volume of blood pumped out by one ventricle in a single beat
x: Stroke volume is the blood ejected by one ventricle per beat (about 70 mL at rest). Multiplying it by the heart rate gives cardiac output per minute.

q: Which valves are open while the atria are contracting?
x: In atrial systole the atrioventricular (tricuspid and bicuspid) valves are open so blood enters the ventricles. The semilunar valves stay closed because the ventricles are relaxed.

q: During ventricular systole, the right and left ventricles contract:
o: One after the other, the right first and then the left
At the same time, sending blood into the pulmonary trunk and aorta together
One after the other, the left first and then the right
x: Both ventricles contract together, so equal volumes of blood are sent into the pulmonary trunk and the aorta in each beat.

q: The atrioventricular valves close at the start of ventricular systole because:
o: Pressure in the aorta rises above pressure in the ventricles
The papillary muscles pull the cusps shut
Pressure in the ventricles rises above pressure in the atria
The atria contract and push the cusps closed
x: As the ventricles contract, their pressure exceeds atrial pressure and pushes the cusps shut. Papillary muscles and chordae only stop the cusps turning inside out; they do not close them.

q: Comparing the two normal heart sounds, the first sound 'lubb' is:
o: Produced while the ventricles are relaxed
Longer and lower in pitch than 'dubb'
x: 'Lubb' is the longer, low-pitched sound of the atrioventricular valves closing. 'Dubb' is shorter and sharper, from the semilunar valves closing.

q: The short interval between the 'lubb' and the 'dubb' sounds corresponds to:
x: 'Lubb' marks the start of ventricular systole and 'dubb' marks its end, so the time between them is the period when the ventricles are contracting.

q: While the whole heart is relaxed, blood flows into the atria from the:
x: During complete diastole the atria fill from the veins: venae cavae on the right and pulmonary veins on the left. The aorta and pulmonary trunk carry blood away from the heart.

q: The SA node is called the pacemaker of the heart because it:
o: Is the largest mass of muscle in the heart
Is the only part of the heart supplied by nerves
Produces impulses at the fastest rate and so sets the rhythm of the whole heart
Delays the impulse between atria and ventricles
x: The SA node fires faster than any other heart tissue, so it starts every beat and sets the heart rate. Delaying the impulse is the job of the AV node.

q: The AV node is situated in the:
o: Wall of the left ventricle near the apex
Upper wall of the left atrium
Lower part of the right atrium, near the interatrial septum
x: The AV node lies in the floor of the right atrium close to the interatrial septum, at the junction of atria and ventricles. The SA node is higher up in the right atrial wall.

q: If the SA node stops working, the heart usually:
o: Stops beating at once and cannot restart
Beats faster because the vagus nerve takes over
Keeps beating, but more slowly, under the control of the AV node
x: Other conducting tissue, especially the AV node, can produce impulses on its own but at a slower rate. So the heart continues beating slowly; nerves only change the rate, they do not start the beat.

q: An artificial pacemaker is fitted in a patient whose:
o: Coronary arteries are narrowed by fat
Heart's own impulse-generating or conducting system does not work properly
x: An artificial pacemaker sends regular electrical impulses to the heart muscle when the natural pacemaker or conduction pathway fails. Leaky valves and blocked arteries need other treatment.

q: A student counts the pulse at her wrist as 72 per minute. Her heart rate is:
o: Impossible to tell from the pulse
x: Each pulse wave is produced by one ventricular contraction, so the pulse rate equals the heart rate.

q: The centre in the brain that adjusts the heart rate through nerves is located in the:
x: The cardiac (cardiovascular) centre is in the medulla oblongata. It sends sympathetic and vagus impulses to speed up or slow down the heart.

q: At rest, the ventricles spend more time in diastole than in systole. This is useful because it:
o: Allows the semilunar valves to stay open longer
Keeps blood pressure in the arteries at zero
Lets the atria and ventricles contract together
Gives the ventricles time to refill and the heart muscle time to rest
x: The long relaxation phase allows the chambers to fill fully and lets the cardiac muscle recover before the next beat, so it does not tire.

q: In a heartbeat of 0.8 second, the atrial muscle contracts for only 0.1 second. The atria therefore rest for:
x: Rest time = 0.8 − 0.1 = 0.7 second. The value 0.5 second is the ventricles' rest time, since ventricular systole lasts 0.3 second.

q: When the heart rate rises during exercise, the length of each cardiac cycle falls. This shortening comes mainly from a shorter:
x: As the heart speeds up, systole shortens only a little; most of the time saved comes from a shorter diastole (the resting and filling phase).

q: The normal heart sounds heard with a stethoscope are produced mainly by the:
o: Flow of blood in the coronary arteries
x: 'Lubb' and 'dubb' are made by the valves snapping shut: first the atrioventricular valves, then the semilunar valves. Muscle contraction and nerve impulses are silent.

q: A doctor hears an extra swishing sound (a murmur) with the heartbeat. A common cause is:
o: A heart rate of 75 beats per minute
Normal closure of the semilunar valves
A heart valve that does not close properly, so blood leaks back
A very slow pulse at the wrist
x: A murmur is an abnormal sound, often from blood leaking backwards through a faulty valve. Normal valve closure gives only the lubb and dubb sounds.

q: While the ventricles are in systole, the atria are:
o: Contracting and pushing blood into the ventricles
Relaxed and filling with blood from the veins
Contracting and pushing blood into the veins
x: Atria and ventricles never contract at the same moment. During ventricular systole the atria are in diastole and refill from the venae cavae and pulmonary veins.

q: Which vessels return blood from the body's organs to the heart?
x: Veins carry blood back towards the heart. Arteries and arterioles carry it away, and lacteals are lymph vessels.

q: Small arteries branch into still smaller vessels that lead into the capillaries. These vessels are:
x: Arteries divide into arterioles, which feed capillaries. Venules collect blood from the capillaries and join to form veins.

q: A network of capillaries supplying a tissue is called a:
x: Capillaries form a branching network, the capillary bed, in every tissue. A portal system is two capillary beds joined by a vein.

q: As blood travels from the aorta to the capillaries, its pressure falls most steeply while it passes through the:
x: Arterioles are narrow and muscular and offer the greatest resistance, so the biggest pressure drop happens there. Pressure in the aorta and large arteries stays high, and the venae cavae come after the capillaries.

q: Which vein carries oxygenated blood?
x: Pulmonary veins bring oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. The other veins carry blood that has already given up oxygen to the tissues.

q: By the classic textbook threshold, a person has high blood pressure (hypertension) when the reading stays at or above about:
x: About 120/80 mmHg is normal for a young adult. In the classic textbook definition, a reading that stays at about 140/90 mmHg or more is taken as hypertension.

q: In a cross-section, a blood vessel has a thin wall and a wide, irregular, partly collapsed lumen. The vessel is:
x: Veins have thin walls with little muscle and elastic tissue, so they collapse when empty. Arteries keep a round lumen, and capillaries are microscopic tubes.

q: Blood capillaries connect:
x: Blood flows from arterioles into capillaries and then into venules. Capillaries do not open into the heart or the lymph ducts.

q: In the capillaries of a working muscle, which substances pass from the blood into the tissue fluid?
o: Plasma proteins and red blood cells
x: Oxygen and nutrients such as glucose diffuse out to the cells. Carbon dioxide and wastes pass the other way, and cells and large proteins stay in the blood.

q: Most plasma proteins stay inside the blood capillaries because they:
o: Are too large to pass through the capillary walls
Are actively pumped back by the endothelium
Are destroyed as soon as they leave
Are bound to the red blood cells
x: Plasma proteins are large molecules that cannot easily cross the capillary wall, so they remain in the blood and create its osmotic pressure.

q: Water re-enters the blood near the venule end of a capillary bed mainly because there:
o: Blood pressure is greater than at the arteriole end
The osmotic pull of plasma proteins is greater than the blood pressure
Valves in the capillary push the water back
The capillary wall becomes impermeable to water
x: Blood pressure falls along the capillary while the osmotic pressure of plasma proteins stays about the same. Near the venule end osmosis wins and water moves back in.

q: Tissue fluid that bathes the body's cells differs from blood plasma mainly in having:
x: Tissue fluid is plasma that has leaked out of capillaries without the large proteins and cells. Its small solutes, like glucose, are at similar levels.

q: Varicose veins, which are swollen and twisted, usually develop when:
o: Fat is deposited inside the arteries
Valves in the veins become weak, so blood collects in the veins
Lymph vessels are blocked by worms
x: When venous valves fail, blood flows back and pools, stretching the vein walls, often in the legs. Fatty deposits in arteries cause atherosclerosis instead.

q: Atherosclerosis is a condition in which:
o: Calcium salts make vein walls brittle
Fatty deposits containing cholesterol build up in artery walls and narrow the lumen
Valves of the veins stop working
The heart muscle becomes inflamed by infection
x: In atherosclerosis, cholesterol-rich plaques form inside arteries, narrowing them and reducing blood flow. Hardening by calcium is described as arteriosclerosis.

q: Arteriosclerosis refers to:
o: Swelling of veins caused by weak valves
Hardening of the artery walls, with loss of their elasticity
x: In arteriosclerosis the artery walls become thick and stiff, often by calcium deposits, so they can no longer stretch and recoil with each beat.

q: Narrowing of arteries by fatty deposits tends to raise blood pressure because:
o: The heart must pump harder to push blood through the narrower vessels
The narrowed arteries pump blood themselves
More plasma leaks into the tissues
The veins become wider and hold more blood
x: A narrower lumen offers more resistance to blood flow, so the heart has to produce a higher pressure to move the same volume of blood.

q: When the arterioles supplying the skin widen (vasodilation) on a hot day:
o: Less blood reaches the skin and heat is kept in
The heart stops pumping blood to the skin
More blood flows near the skin surface and more heat is lost
Blood moves from the skin into the veins of the gut
x: Relaxed arteriole muscle widens the vessels, sending more warm blood near the skin surface so heat is lost. Narrowing (vasoconstriction) does the opposite.

q: The carotid arteries supply blood to the:
x: The carotid arteries run up the neck to the head and brain. The arms are supplied by the subclavian arteries and the kidneys by the renal arteries.

q: A band is tied fairly tightly around the upper arm, and the veins below it swell. This happens because:
o: Blood still enters through the deep arteries but cannot leave through the squeezed veins
The band forces blood backwards from the heart into the arm
The arteries below the band burst
The valves in the arm veins open wider
x: Thin-walled veins are compressed easily, but the deeper high-pressure arteries keep supplying blood. Blood enters and cannot get out, so the veins fill and bulge.

q: Which of these vessels has NO valves?
x: Capillaries are tiny tubes of a single cell layer with no valves. Limb veins and lymph vessels have valves that stop backflow.

q: A pulse can be felt in arteries but not in veins because:
o: Veins carry no blood between heartbeats
Veins have stiffer walls than arteries
Blood flows away from the heart in veins
The pressure surges are smoothed out before blood reaches the veins
x: Pressure waves from each ventricular contraction are damped in the arterioles and capillaries, so blood in veins flows steadily at low pressure.

q: Compared with blood in the main artery of the arm, blood in a vein of the arm is:
o: Poorer in oxygen and richer in carbon dioxide
Richer in oxygen and poorer in carbon dioxide
x: The arm tissues take oxygen from the blood and add carbon dioxide, so the returning venous blood has less oxygen. It is under lower pressure and moves towards the heart.

q: Blood pressure is normally measured on the:
o: Brachial artery of the upper arm
x: The cuff of the sphygmomanometer is wrapped round the upper arm to measure pressure in the brachial artery, which is at about the level of the heart.

q: Which organ is NOT part of the lymphatic system?
x: The spleen, thymus and tonsils are lymphoid organs. The pancreas is a digestive and endocrine gland.

q: Lymph from all over the body is finally collected into two large vessels, the:
o: Hepatic portal vein and thoracic duct
Thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct
x: Lymph vessels join to form two main ducts, the thoracic duct and the right lymphatic duct, which empty lymph into the veins near the neck.

q: Lymph enters a lymph node and leaves it through vessels called, respectively, the:
x: Several afferent vessels bring lymph into a node and fewer efferent vessels carry the filtered lymph out.

q: In the villi, digested fats enter the lacteals mainly as:
o: Tiny fat droplets coated with protein (chylomicrons)
x: Fatty acids and glycerol are rebuilt into fat inside intestinal cells and leave as protein-coated droplets (chylomicrons), which are too large for blood capillaries and enter the lacteals.

q: The largest lymphoid organ of the human body is the:
x: The spleen is the largest single mass of lymphoid tissue. The thymus, tonsils and appendix are much smaller.

q: Besides its role after birth, the spleen in the fetus also:
x: Before birth the spleen is one of the sites where red blood cells are made. After birth this job passes to the red bone marrow.

q: During a severe loss of blood, the spleen can help because it:
o: Produces new plasma proteins at once
Pumps blood like a second heart
Stores a reserve of blood that it can release into circulation
x: The spleen holds a reserve of blood. When blood is lost, it can contract and send this blood into the circulation.

q: After the spleen is removed because of injury, a person can live normally but is more likely to:
x: The spleen filters blood and helps fight blood-borne bacteria, so without it some infections become more likely. Bone marrow, the thymus and fat digestion are not affected.

q: The thymus helps lymphocytes become mature T cells partly by secreting the hormone:
x: The thymus releases thymosin, which promotes the maturation of T-lymphocytes. Thyroxine comes from the thyroid gland, a different organ.

q: Infection and swelling of the tonsils is called:
x: Inflammation of the tonsils is tonsillitis. Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix, and elephantiasis is caused by blocked lymph vessels.

q: The adenoids are lymphoid tissue found at the:
o: Junction of the small and large intestines
Back of the nasal cavity, above the throat
x: Adenoids (pharyngeal tonsils) sit at the back of the nose where it joins the throat, trapping pathogens that are breathed in.

q: Which part of the digestive tract contains a large amount of lymphoid tissue?
x: The appendix wall is rich in lymphoid tissue. The gall bladder stores bile, and the oesophagus and pancreatic duct are not lymphoid structures.

q: Compared with veins, lymph vessels have:
o: Muscular walls that beat like a heart
x: Lymph vessels resemble veins but are thinner walled and have even more valves. They have no pump of their own.

q: Each day, the lymphatic system returns to the blood about:
o: A few litres (about 3 litres) of fluid
x: Of the fluid that leaves the blood capillaries daily, roughly 3 litres is not reabsorbed and is returned by the lymph vessels.

q: Cancer cells from a tumour in the breast often reach the lymph nodes of the armpit first. This is because:
o: Armpit nodes produce the cancer cells
Lymph from the breast drains through the armpit nodes
Arteries carry cancer cells directly into the armpit
The thoracic duct begins in the armpit
x: Lymph from the breast passes through the armpit (axillary) nodes, so cells that escape into lymph are often trapped there first.

q: Unlike blood, lymph has no heart to pump it. As a result, lymph flows:
o: Faster than blood in the arteries
In both directions in each vessel
Only when a person is asleep
x: With no pump, lymph moves slowly at low pressure, helped by muscle movements, with valves keeping it flowing one way.

q: Within a lymph node, bacteria are engulfed and digested mainly by:
x: Macrophages in the lymph nodes are phagocytes that engulf bacteria and debris filtered from the lymph. Red cells and platelets do not.

q: Which is a secondary lymphoid organ, where mature lymphocytes meet antigens?
x: Bone marrow and thymus are primary organs where lymphocytes form or mature. Lymph nodes (and the spleen) are secondary organs where mature lymphocytes meet antigens.

q: Tissue fluid enters lymph capillaries easily because their walls:
o: Have overlapping endothelial cells that act as one-way flaps
Contain pumps that pull fluid in
Are lined with red blood cells
x: The endothelial cells of lymph capillaries overlap loosely, opening inward to let fluid in but closing to stop it leaking out.

q: Normal lymph from the arms and legs is:
x: Lymph is a clear, pale fluid because it has no red blood cells. Only lymph from the gut after a fatty meal (chyle) looks milky.

q: Unlike absorbed glucose, absorbed fats reach the general blood circulation without passing first through the liver. This is because fats:
o: Enter lacteals and travel in lymph to the veins near the neck
Are carried in the hepatic portal vein
Are absorbed directly through the stomach wall
Are broken down to glucose in the villi
x: Glucose enters blood capillaries and travels in the hepatic portal vein to the liver. Fats enter lacteals and travel in the lymph to the thoracic duct, which joins a vein in the neck.

q: Before lymph is returned to the blood, it normally passes through:
o: The kidneys, where it is cleaned
One or more lymph nodes, where it is filtered
The heart, where it is pumped
The liver, where it is detoxified
x: Lymph vessels pass through lymph nodes, which filter out pathogens and debris before the lymph reaches the ducts and veins.
